conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning, I'm Dr. Lee. I understand you came in with chest pressure last night?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it woke me up. Felt just like my heart attack before. I took nitroglycerin, but it didn’t help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You also said it got worse when you took a deep breath?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. I couldn’t catch a full breath, but I wasn’t short of breath. Just pressure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve reviewed your EKG and your troponin levels—both are normal. That’s good news. It doesn’t look like a heart attack.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, thank goodness. But what is it then?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re considering inflammation around the heart—called pericarditis. It can cause sharp chest pain that worsens with breathing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Pericarditis? Is that related to my recent pneumonia?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, exactly. Viral infections like the parainfluenza you had can sometimes lead to post-viral pericarditis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not my heart muscle, but the lining around it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s right. And we’ve ruled out other causes—your chest X-ray was clear, and a V/Q scan showed no pulmonary embolism.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the ultrasound on my legs?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No blood clots. That’s reassuring, especially with your history of DVT and PE.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I was worried about that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We also did an echocardiogram. Your heart function is stable—about 43% ejection fraction, mostly unchanged from before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And no fluid around the heart?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No pericardial effusion. That’s another good sign.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what’s the plan?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re going to start you on a steroid—prednisone—to reduce the inflammation. It usually works well for pericarditis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been on steroids before. Will it affect my kidney?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll monitor closely. Your transplant team is aware. We’re starting low and tapering slowly to minimize risks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How’s the chest pain today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better. Still there, but not as intense. I think the prednisone is helping.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great to hear. Your labs this morning show your kidney function is stable, though creatinine is a bit higher—2.5 from 2.0.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that from the steroid?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. We’ll keep an eye on it. Your potassium was low yesterday, so we gave you some, and it’s improved.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember that. Felt a bit weak.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, low potassium can do that. We’ll keep monitoring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My mouth feels dry. And I noticed some little sores on the roof of my mouth.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I’ll take a look. Sometimes steroids or viral infections can cause oral changes. We’ll make sure it’s not an infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your pain is continuing to improve, and your breathing is easier?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, much better. I’m even walking in the hall a little.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Excellent. We’re going to keep you on the prednisone taper. You’re on day three of 20 mg, then we’ll step down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my other meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Most are continuing. We’ve held amlodipine because your blood pressure has been well-controlled—around 130s over 80.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And the zolpidem?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve switched you to trazodone for sleep. It’s safer with your other medications.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been on that before. It worked well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing really well. Pain is minimal, labs are stable. We’re planning for discharge tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What about follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll need a new cardiologist—your previous one has left the practice. You’re scheduled to see a nurse practitioner next week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll make sure to call and confirm.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Also, please get a Chem 7 blood test done in a few days and send the results to your primary doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll do that. Any restrictions at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take it easy for a few days. No heavy lifting. Continue the prednisone exactly as prescribed—don’t stop suddenly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I won’t. I know how that goes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All set for discharge. Your pain is resolved, and you’re back to your baseline.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I was really scared it was another heart attack.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. But everything points to pericarditis, and you’ve responded well. Keep taking the steroids, and call if the chest pain returns.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And I’ll follow up with the NP and get the blood work done.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. You’re doing great. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Dr. Lee.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You're welcome. Someone will be in shortly with your discharge papers.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. I’m ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll make sure your sister knows you’re on your way.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: She’s been worried. I’ll call her right after.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a good idea. Stay in touch with your care team, and take it easy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You're very welcome. Get some rest and we’ll see you in follow-up.
